transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-01
Time: 15:00 UTC (approx)
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Verdant Head of ML), Samir Das (Verdant Platform Eng), Olivia Park (Verdant CTO)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to validate fit for rehosting Verdant's inference layer. Focus on eval parity, vLLM/TGI compatibility, networking/VPC requirements, and security. Action items captured.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for making time — Maya from Redwood, I run the AE motion with Verdant folks. Quick intro?
[00:10] Lena Ortiz: Hey Maya, Lena here. I'm the Head of ML at Verdant, been running model infra and evaluation.
[00:15] Samir Das: Samir, platform eng — infra, k8s, on prem-ish stuff, hybrid clouds.
[00:20] Olivia Park: Olivia, CTO, mostly listening for risk and timelines.
[00:25] Maya Chen: And Ravi is our SE, he'll lead the tech deep-dive. Ravi?
[00:30] Ravi Patel: Thanks. Quick agenda: 1) understand current stack and pain, 2) compatibility concerns (vLLM/TGI), 3) hosting options and security, 4) next steps. Ok?

[02:10] Lena Ortiz: We currently run on a managed provider, basically a mix of OpenAI and a self-hosted vLLM/TGI layer for specific models. The managed provider is convenient but creeping costs and tail latencies in heavy traffic are biting. We also see regression risk when they update model variants. Our eval metrics slipped twice in the last quarter after provider upgrades.

[04:05] Maya Chen: Understood. When you say "regression" — is that quality drop or hallucination increase?
[04:12] Lena Ortiz: Both. It's small but significant on our safety prompts. We have a test-suite of ~1k prompts and we run nightly evals. After a provider model swap, a few hundred samples changed classification. That's the parity worry — can you run the same prompts and show parity?

[06:20] Ravi Patel: Absolutely, parity is standard we run for prospects. We usually request your eval set, run both the managed provider and Redwood hosted with the same model versions or closest equivalents, and compare metrics (exact match, ROUGE/F1, hallucination flags). Our bench will also capture latency p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens. Are you able to share a sanitized prompt set?

[08:00] Samir Das: We can share a sanitized set, yes. Also we need to know how you manage model variants — like can we pin exact model hashes/versions? We've had providers auto-upgrade.

[09:30] Ravi Patel: You can pin model versions in Redwood. For hosted we maintain curated model catalog; customers can request version pinning for their team. Dedicated/private gives you even stronger controls — pinned images and rollout gating.

[11:45] Olivia Park: Important for us: data residency and audit trails. If we go dedicated or private, what do audit logs look like and how do you integrate with our KMS?

[12:10] Maya Chen: Short answer: we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, Hashicorp Vault, HSMs via partners) for private deployments; hosted offers managed encryption with BYOK options. Audit logs and token-level traces are available in the console and can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll send docs after the call.

[13:05] Lena Ortiz: Also SSO and RBAC — we need SAML at minimum and role separation for dev vs ops.

[13:20] Ravi Patel: We support SAML/SSO and fine-grained RBAC. For Dedicated and Private you can sync groups via SCIM. For Hosted we have enterprise SSO with SCIM and RBAC on top.

[15:00] Samir Das: A big technical blocker is our network topology. We run on a hybrid cloud with on-prem GPUs behind a firewall. Can Redwood run in our VPC or air-gapped?

[15:20] Ravi Patel: For on-prem we offer the Private deployment model — a customer-managed control plane or full on-prem package. There are two paths: 1) Private with customer VPC and control plane in a partner region, or 2) fully air-gapped on-prem package for regulated data. We'd need to map out egress rules and NAT requirements.

[18:00] Lena Ortiz: Ok. On compatibility — we lean heavily on vLLM/TGI stacks and a custom quantized runtime (4-bit) for latency. Can Redwood run our vLLM-optimized models? We need to keep performance.

[19:12] Ravi Patel: Short: yes, but with nuances. Our runtime supports models exported for TGI/vLLM with a compatibility layer. For quantized configs we support 8-bit and 4-bit on certain GPUs — we have quantization-aware execution paths. We also do kernel selection per architecture. We'll need an example model artifact and a small benchmark run. Some model ops (custom kernels) might require us to help onboard or add a kernel — usually doable in the onboarding sprint.

[21:30] Samir Das: Do you preserve the KV cache across calls for conversational use? We currently use prefix/KV cache heavily to keep latency low.

[21:45] Ravi Patel: Yes — continuous KV cache and prefix caching are supported. On Dedicated we can tune cache sizes and memory placement. On hosted we have sensible defaults and cache warming. We can also export and import KV checkpoints during migration.

[24:00] Lena Ortiz: What about streaming and function/tool-calls? Our app uses streaming tokens and structured function outputs heavily.

[24:12] Maya Chen: Redwood supports streaming responses, function/tool calling, and structured outputs. The API is compatible with most SDKs; we'll share examples.

[26:35] Olivia Park: Let's talk costs briefly. If we move from pay-as-you-go (managed provider) to Redwood Dedicated, what's the break-even? We're looking for predictable throughput but not overcommitting.

[27:00] Ravi Patel: We do committed monthly for Dedicated but offer burst and overflow to hosted in case of spikes. We can run a cost model — take your current token consumption and latency SLOs and we'll propose Dedicated vs Hosted blended option. We'll show unit economics with different quantization profiles.

[30:15] Samir Das: I want to flag that our infra team will insist on a security review. Do you have an SOC 2 report and a pen test summary?

[30:30] Maya Chen: Yes, we can share SOC 2 Type II and recent pentest summary under NDA. We'll attach compliance pack.

[32:50] Lena Ortiz: On benchmarks: we need not just accuracy parity but also behavioral/regression tests. Can you integrate with our eval harness and run nightly differential tests?

[33:05] Ravi Patel: We can integrate. Typical flow: you give us harness and baseline outputs, we run parity and produce diffs and a quality report. We can trigger regression alerts if metrics cross thresholds. Redwood Optimize also suggests quantization profiles and batching to meet cost/latency targets.

[36:45] Samir Das: One operational question — how do model rollouts work? If we deploy a new model version, can we canary and roll back automatically?

[37:00] Ravi Patel: Yes — rollouts support canary percentages, A/B routing, and automatic fallback policies. In Dedicated/private you can control rollout gates; Hosted has automatic safety fallbacks.

[40:20] Olivia Park: Timeline is critical. If we greenlight a pilot, how fast can we get a hosted parity run and a Dedicated POC?

[40:35] Maya Chen: Hosted parity run can start within a week once we have artifacts and the prompt set. Dedicated POC or Private can be scoped quickly but usually takes 4–8 weeks depending on on-prem/networking needs.

[42:10] Lena Ortiz: A few nitty things: logging retention for us is 12 months, and we need the ability to scrub PII from logs. Also we have compliance requirements around data residency in EU.

[42:30] Ravi Patel: Log retention is configurable on Dedicated/Private; hosted enterprise has extended retention add-on. For PII we can mask logs and integrate with your data loss prevention tooling. For EU residency we can schedule workloads in EU regions.

[45:00] Samir Das: On the technical parity bench: can you run both vLLM/TGI-backed local variant and Redwood's hosted variant side-by-side and output token-level diffs? We need a deterministic comparison.

[45:25] Ravi Patel: Yes. We'll run side-by-side with the same seed/temperature settings and produce token-level deltas, hallucination markers, and metric summaries. We'll use your harness. Expect initial run in 3–5 business days after we get artifacts.

[48:00] Lena Ortiz: Anything you need from us to get started?

[48:05] Maya Chen: The main items: 1) sanitized prompt set and eval harness, 2) example model artifacts (or pointers to current models), 3) current usage metrics and latency p50/p95/p99, 4) contact for infra deep-dive (Samir).

[49:30] Samir Das: I'll package those and send them. Also I'll list our VPC peering / firewall rules.

[50:10] Olivia Park: If we move forward, we'll want a short-run pilot on Hosted to validate parity before committing to Dedicated. That reduces risk.

[50:30] Maya Chen: Makes sense and that's the standard path many take. We'll do hosted parity first and then scope Dedicated if results are good.

[51:00] Maya Chen: Quick recap and next steps: Maya to send pricing and compliance pack, Ravi to share benchmark plan and schedule, Samir to share artifacts and infra diagram. We'll reconvene after first parity run. Any objections?

[51:20] Lena Ortiz: No objections. Sounds good.
[51:35] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with docs and calendar invites.

End of transcript.
